edibilityNotes: Toxic. Causes severe acute gastrointestinal poisoning (vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps), typically beginning 30 minutes to 2 hours after ingestion. Rarely fatal in otherwise healthy adults, but it is one of the more common causes of serious mushroom poisoning in Europe; severe dehydration and electrolyte loss can be dangerous for children, the elderly, and those with underlying conditions. The toxins are not fully characterized and are not destroyed by cooking. Never eat this species.
description: Entoloma sinuatum, the livid entoloma or livid pinkgill, is a large, robust mushroom of the family Entolomataceae with a pale grey-tan to ivory-buff cap. The cap is fleshy and broadly convex to flattened, often with a low umbo and a smooth, slightly silky surface, commonly 7-20 cm across. The gills are adnexed to sinuate (emarginate), starting pale yellowish or cream and maturing to a distinctive salmon-pink as the spores ripen. The stout, fibrous stipe is white and lacks a ring. The flesh has a mealy/farinaceous smell. A defining feature is the pink spore print, produced by the angular (polygonal) basidiospores typical of the genus. It fruits in summer and autumn, usually in deciduous (broadleaf) woodland favoring oak and beech, on heavy clay or calcareous soils. It is the type species of Entoloma and a leading cause of serious gastrointestinal mushroom poisoning across Europe, owing to its resemblance to several edible species.
distribution: Widespread across Europe; also reported in temperate North America and parts of Asia.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Clitopilus prunulus (The Miller)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible but easily confused, and a frequent source of poisonings. The Miller is much smaller, with strongly decurrent gills (running down the stem), a strong mealy smell, and a pinkish (paler) spore print. Entoloma sinuatum is far larger with sinuate/adnexed gills that are not decurrent.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Calocybe gambosa (St George's Mushroom)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Edible. Fruits in spring (around St George's Day, late April), whereas E. sinuatum appears in summer/autumn. Calocybe gambosa has a WHITE spore print and crowded white gills, versus the pink gills and pink spore print of E. sinuatum.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Agaricus species (young button mushrooms)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Young Agaricus can resemble the pale cap. Agaricus has free gills that turn pink then chocolate-brown to blackish, a DARK BROWN spore print, and usually a ring on the stem. E. sinuatum gills stay salmon-pink, its spore print is pink (never brown), and it has no ring.
